content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper introduces a new self-supervised method for learning representations of gigapixel microscopy images, called whole-slide images (WSIs). This is a challenging vision task because the images are of sizes on average of 93,000 pixels by 67,500 pixels. The standard approach in the field is to use multiple instance learning (MIL), where tiles of the image are embedded and bags of tiles are later processed. Although the performance of MIL is strong for datasets with many thousands of WSIs, it does not perform as well for datasets with only hundreds of slides.

For this reason the present manuscript turns to self-supervised learning due to its strong performance in sample-starved settings. The approach is designed to scale to the very large size of WSIs. First, a WSI is split into tiles. A pretrained ResNet18 extracts embeddings from each tile. Then, a pooling operator (sparse ResNet18) aggregates the embeddings across the WSI into a final feature vector. The pooling operator is trained with momentum contrast self-supervision, while the patch extractor ResNet18 can be pretrained on either ImageNet or in-domain with WSIs.

At inference time the output from the pooling operator is provided to a logistic regression framework for calculating the final classifications. Since a fixed number of tiles were used for training the sparse ResNet18 (the chosen pooling operator of this paper), the same number of tiles has to be used at inference time - this prompted the manuscript to also develop an ensemble strategy where bags of tiles are bootstrapped from a single WSI, and the average over the bootstrap ensemble is used as the input to the logistic regression.

The manuscript’s contributions include:
1. An SSL method that can scale to the Giga-Pixel regime.
2. SotA performance on several tasks using WSIs
3. Public release of the embeddings of the Cancer-Genome Atlas (TCGA), which in total take only 23 Mb as opposed to the 16 Tb of the original dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The performance of the method seems to be strong (on average) in both the large-sample and low-sample regimes. On the other hand, some aspects of the paper, mostly related to clarity and the reporting of the results, make it more difficult to evaluate vs. other methods. Specifics below:

**Strengths**
1. Manuscript introduces an SSL method that scales well to very large whole-slide images.
2. SotA performance across several tasks from a major dataset, as well as strong performance in sample-starved regimes.
3. Release of the embeddings for the Cancer-Genome Atlas (TCGA) dataset.
4. Detailed ablations over several design choice parameters, including:
(a) Whether or not to share augmentations for tiles within a WSI
(b) Whether to use ImageNet or in-domain data for pretraining the embedding extractor.
(c) Measurements of model performance on a variety of sampling regimes.
(d) Ensembling strategies and numbers of tiles to use therein.

**Weaknesses**
1. The use of the word “compression” for the released dataset is not ideal. The manuscript’s representation of the data has thrown away much information, including, by definition, information in the data that may be related to any aspect of the augmentations such as color jitter. As such, I question the use of the word “compression” as the compressed representations may be missing quite a bit of what was in the original data. Certainly, one cannot reconstruct the original data with the representations. The manuscript is also lacking in an information-theoretic analysis of the representations such as that by Dubois et al. in “Lossy Compression for Lossless Prediction” (2021). I would generally prefer an alternative word for what the manuscript is doing to TCGA. It is producing representations, and the representations are what is being released.
2. There are several issues with paper organization clarity. For example, in Section 4.1 under “Datasets” almost the entire paragraph is dedicated to methodological descriptions rather than the data. This is important because at ICLR many readers may not have the background to understand the data and tasks. Less related to data, but perhaps more critically, I’m not sure which parts of Giga-SSL are novel. Is it the augmentations, the embedding extraction, the pooling, or the use of a higher-level MoCo? The manuscript claims the entire model as a novelty, but other papers have used some of these components. More clarity on the novelty of the model and the descriptions of the data would help readers. It is fine if the manuscript’s novelty is the sum of its parts, but in this case more specific references could help in showing where the parts come from vs. how summarizing them is new. For example, be sure to reference previous papers that used MoCo for patch embeddings, and ideally reference previous work on tile aggregation modules. The manuscript says there has been a lot of work on pooling, but doesn’t say much about what work was done.
3. The manuscript only evaluates on one dataset, and as such the evaluations have no domain-shift. Domain shift is a major topic within the field of computational histopathology, but to the manuscript’s credit this is already listed in the limitation section. Other medical image analysis papers may also include some validation with human annotators, and this could be another limitation.
4. The manuscript does not examine the effects of sample selection. The average ROC AUC scores are the only metric used. The manuscript should have confidence intervals on the AUC scores (and the other metrics presented) to give an idea of how much sample noise is a factor in the results. As an alternative other papers in medical image analysis use bootstrapping.
5. ROC AUC is the only metric examined. AUC is known to have some flaws, and predictive analytics departments at hospitals may desire to know other metrics such as precision-recall (with related areas under curve) or c-indices.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Much of this was already summarized in my comments on strengths and weaknesses. I think the originality and clarity could both use some clarification by the authors. I think there has been some effort already on this in the manuscript, but it could be a bit better organized. In particular, I would like:
1.  To understand whether any of the components (such as MoCo tile embeddings) have been proposed previously, and whether the sum of the parts of Giga-SSL are its primary novelty, or whether there are a number of subcomponents that are the novelties.
2. The authors to strengthen their statistical analysis of the proposed methods to better-incorporate some well-known challenges in the computational histopathology field.

If these were all improved I may be able to improve my recommendation.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proses SSL-based approach to represent whole slide images (WSI). The paper shows that the SSL representations could potentially be used as compressed representations of WSIs. The paper reports that the obtained representations could reduce the storage requirements for TCGA dataset from terabits to megabits while maintaining important pathology information and achieving good downstream task performances.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The paper deals with a relevant problem of WSI compression.
- The paper reports promising results.

Weaknesses (see details below):
- The presentation of the paper should be improved
- The positioning of the paper w.r.t prior art should be better articulated.
- Unclear novelty
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The clarity of presentations should be significantly improved. Below are some suggestions. 

- Introduction: How the proposed pipeline positions itself w.r.t. other SSL-based representations. Please clarify. The clarification should appear in the paragraph starting with “Here, we propose Giga-SSL, a strategy to perform SSL for Gigapixel images.”. Clarifying why given the literature in Section 2.3. one should represent the WSI with a feature vector from the SSL based model would be a good idea.

- Introduction: Adding a statement addressing what do we learn as a research community from the experiments conducted in the paper would strengthen the intro. What the published results change in WSI? What is the reflection of these results on broader ML community?

- Introduction: Introduction positions the paper in a large part by contrasting the introduced pipeline w.r.t. MIL however, based on Fig. 1 the introduced Giga-SSL also requires an aggregation model such as MIL. Thus, the current positioning of the intro is somehow misleading. Could the authors clarify? Does it mean that the introduced Giga-SSL also inherits the strengths and drawbacks of MIL?

- Introduction: The large amount of noise thus often leads to overfitting and poor performance. <- Unclear, could the authors clarify this statement?

- Introduction: Dealing with WSI is technically demanding. <- Could the authors be more specific? What are the technical challenges beyond WSI resolution?

- Introduction: “the performances remain highly dependent on the size of the training dataset” <- In MIL setup the performance would also depend on the feature extractor used to represent each patch.

- Introduction: Indeed, MIL performance reaches saturation when using thousands of slides with associated ground truth for training. <- Could the authors provide a reference for this statement?

- Introduction: On the other hand <- Please add on the one hand in the text too. Currently the text is a bit unclear.

- Introduction/Methodology: From the current text it is unclear what are the novel elements in the proposed pipeline. Please clarify.

- Section 2.2 could be removed or moved to appendix.

- Figure 1, please clarify in the caption or in the Figure what T, F and \theta mean.

- The methodology section is unclear. The section should be rewritten focusing on clarity of model presentation.

- Methodology: The tile encoder seems to be pretrained. If a tile encoder is pretrained on a supervised tasks thus the method might not be fully self-supervised? Is it feasible to train the whole pipeline from scratch? Could the authors provide details on the datasets used to pretrain the tail encoder?

- Methodology: Giga-SSL pipeline seems to be trained with a contrastive loss. However, the loss is not specified in the main body of the paper. Please include the training objective formulation in the methodology section.

- Please correct the formatting of figures and tables to ensure they follow ICLR format.

- Experiments: Which aggregation was used for Giga-SSL in the results reported in table 2.

- Experiments: Please add std due to random seed in tables 2 and 3.

- Experiments: Why were all Giga-SSL models trained for 1000 epochs?

Quality: The paper’s current presentation makes it hard to judge the quality well. 

Novelty: The reviewer is not an expert in the field of WSI classification. However, based on the current paper presentation it is hard to pinpoint the paper novelty - the SSL has already been applied to WSI. The paper reports good results on downstream tasks that could give some edge of experimental novelty.

Reproducibility: There is no mentioning of the code release. Based on the current paper presentations, the reviewer suspects it would be rather hard to reproduce the reported results. Thus, the reviewer would encourage the authors to rewrite the methodological and experimental sections focusing on explanation simplicity and presentation clarity.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a way of compressing large WSI images by converting them into suitably trained embedding spaces. The authors claim that their technique can compress a dataset as large as 16TB into a mere 23MB, which retains enough information to have SOTA or close to SOTA performance on various benchmark tasks. 
Technically, the manuscript proposes a contrastive learning approach, paired with suitably chosen data augmentation tricks. The different augmented views of the data are first converted into an initial embedding space and then a pooling operator aggregates these embeddings into a single embedding. These final embeddings are then trained via contrastive learning, such that embeddings belonging to the same sample are pulled together, and consequently, the embeddings from different samples are pushed apart. 
To reduce overhead during training, the initial embeddings from different augmented views are precomputed and stored. The manuscript shows experiments on the TGCA cancer dataset and also shows that the proposed method performs at least equal at various downstream processing tasks of cancer subtype detection. 
The manuscript also justifies its method by using different ablation analyses and shows that its method is effective in both standard and low data regimes (compared compared to baseline methods).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The manuscript addresses an important area in WSI image analysis. WSI images are huge and often unannotated which makes them very difficult to be used in a supervised learning setting. This manuscript makes an honest attempt to improve this situation better.
2. The authors use a standard dataset and compress it in form of meaningful embeddings that others could easily use.
3. The authors validate the claims on the downstream classification task of various benchmark cancer subtypes and show that their method performs better.
4. Their method also performs better in a low-data regime.
5. Ablation analysis shows the effectiveness of the proposed compression pipeline.

Weaknesses/Errors:

1. The steps outlined in sec. 3.1 and FIg.1 are not in sync. It is difficult to identify X1 and X2.
2. Steps say that views are created first but Fig 2. shows the augmented view in slide-level augmentation. The things here are not clear.
3. There is no clear explanation to use a pretrained ResNet. It is not clear if the pipeline is agnostic to the choice of the network at the initial embedding generation setting.
4. On page 8, “The fewer tiles the better” paragraph is referring to Fig. 3.A and not 3.B
5. On page 9, in the paragraph “Attention-deep-MIL unlearns…” – on line 5, it is unclear what “2” stands for here.
6. The entire pipeline is shown on the TGCA dataset, so the question remains of how effective will it be for other large datasets.
7. There is no clear description or timeline of how the authors plan to make the embeddings available to the community. Also, there is no mention of making the code available for the community, which I believe should happen!
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: In general the paper is clearly written. However, it is advised that the authors improve their main figures. Overall, I believe the paper proposes novel work of good quality. The level the proposed system is described seems adequate.
content.summary_of_the_review: The presented work addresses an important topic: the tackling of very large and often unannotated WSI datasets. The method uses self-supervised contrastive learning to create embeddings that are much smaller in size and can then easily be used easily. There are minor mistakes in the paper and the main figure should improve. More than the individual parts in the pipeline, the paper overall pipeline has the potential to become a standard in the field. However, the manuscript fails to convince me about why I should trust that the setup will generalize well to other datasets.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors propose handling gigapixel WSI images in a self-supervised learning framework. The de facto approach towards handling large scale Whole Slide Imaging data has been to rely on multi-instance learning with a bag of patches approach. Current MIL approaches, due to reliance on a set of discrete patches, are often not able to learn spatial relationships between features apparent on whole slides, with the extent of such relationships not usually known a priori. This poses a challenge in digital pathology in terms of handling large WSI datasets for a range of tasks where extensive annotation is expensive and impractical. Further, it is often not feasible to load entire gigapixel WSIs onto GPUs for processing, making it difficult to design typical deep neural networks for direct representation learning tasks. The contributions as stated by the authors are:
• a self-supervised contrastive learning framework for Gigapixels images.
• WSI embeddings of the whole TCGA dataset, compressing it by a factor of
almost 1 million from 16Tb to 23Mb
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
While the claims of enabling self-supervised learning for whole slide images would indeed excite the digital pathology community given the dearth of literature on the topic, the exact methodology proposed raises concerns. The whole slide images are divided into tiles, in two copies of the WSI. This is followed by tile-level augmentation, and aggregation, followed by a contrastive objective function. What is not clear to me is a) how is the spatial relationship over multiple tiles preserved or indeed accounted for when augmentations are separately performed, and is followed by an aggregation step involving a pooling operator ( pooling operations are not useful for retaining contextual relationships) b) It is stated that a tile-level augmentation operator transforms each sampled tile. These transformations can be applied either independently to all the tiles (not shared) or the same transformation can be applied to all tiles sampled from the same view (shared). In that case, how is it ensured that the contrastive operation refers to the same tile in the whole slide? The mechanism of ensuring this is not clear from the text. Figure 1 is confusing in this regard - it appears that every patch from the two views is fused into the encoder, and then we see two separate 'embeddings' feeding to the contrastive objectives. It is not clear what is the intended process here - are there representations being created using patches from both the views? Or is the intent to create representations from augmentations of corresponding patches from the two different views? In the former case, the spatial relationship is unlikely to be retained. If it's the latter, the role of the ResNet 18 architecture looks superfluous unless a cumulative embedding needs to be created. The only benefit in that specific case would be the saving in computational time required for the contrastive augmentation step, but the subsequent fusion of the patches doesn't seem to be aligned with the augmentations performed.

While the initiative to provide TCGA embeddings is a good one and can be seen as a contribution to the community for certain tasks, it is to be noted that most tasks in pathology quite dependent on the nature of the datasets and acquisition protocols. A significant issue with models trained on one dataset can fail to generalise to a different data distribution, where such a difference may crop up from even marginal variations in the hematoxilin and eosin staining. Thus, while the representations may be useful as good initializations for learning some tasks, it may be worth being realistic about the utility of such a set of representations and provide an adequate discussion on the shortcomings of this (beyond the limited point made about why explainability is not possible when using such frozen embeddings). Also, a discussion on the computational aspects of the implementation would be appreciated, since a key premise of the paper is to mitigate the computational expenses associated with handling large WSI datasets directly.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clarity is an issue to an extent, as described earlier. Reproducibility may be checked with released codebases as the TCGA dataset is available publicly. The novelty is unclear since patching followed by augmentation has been used in self-supervised learning in earlier work, although not when dealing with gigapixel H&E data.
content.summary_of_the_review:
While the claims of enabling self-supervised learning for whole slide images would indeed excite the digital pathology community given the dearth of literature on the topic, the exact methodology proposed raises concerns. The whole slide images are divided into tiles, in two copies of the WSI. This is followed by tile-level augmentation, and aggregation, followed by a contrastive objective function. What is not clear to me is a) how is the spatial relationship over multiple tiles preserved or indeed accounted for when augmentations are separately performed, and is followed by an aggregation step involving a pooling operator ( pooling operations are not useful for retaining contextual relationships) b) It is stated that a tile-level augmentation operator transforms each sampled tile. These transformations can be applied either independently to all the tiles (not shared) or the same transformation can be applied to all tiles sampled from the same view (shared). In that case, how is it ensured that the contrastive operation refers to the same tile in the whole slide? The mechanism of ensuring this is not clear from the text. Figure 1 is confusing in this regard - it appears that every patch from the two views is fused into the encoder, and then we see two separate 'embeddings' feeding to the contrastive objectives. It is not clear what is the intended process here - are there representations being created using patches from both the views? Or is the intent to create representations from augmentations of corresponding patches from the two different views? In the former case, the spatial relationship is unlikely to be retained. If it's the latter, the role of the ResNet 18 architecture looks superfluous unless a cumulative embedding needs to be created. The only benefit in that specific case would be the saving in computational time required for the contrastive augmentation step, but the subsequent fusion of the patches doesn't seem to be aligned with the augmentations performed.

While the initiative to provide TCGA embeddings is a good one and can be seen as a contribution to the community for certain tasks, it is to be noted that most tasks in pathology quite dependent on the nature of the datasets and acquisition protocols. A significant issue with models trained on one dataset can fail to generalise to a different data distribution, where such a difference may crop up from even marginal variations in the hematoxilin and eosin staining. Thus, while the representations may be useful as good initializations for learning some tasks, it may be worth being realistic about the utility of such a set of representations and provide an adequate discussion on the shortcomings of this (beyond the limited point made about why explainability is not possible when using such frozen embeddings). Also, a discussion on the computational aspects of the implementation would be appreciated, since a key premise of the paper is to mitigate the computational expenses associated with handling large WSI datasets directly.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a slide-level self-supervised learning (SSL) strategy to aggregate tile-level representations in WSI into a slide-level one. The tile-level features are extracted using existing self-supervised pre-trained models. By applying a contrastive loss to two aggregated representations of two different views from a single gigapixel image, the proposed Giga-SSL achieves consistent improves on six datasets, especially when with limited supervision (i.e., tiny datasets). The ablation studies are included to demonstrate the impacts of augmentations and pre-trained models. Besides, the authors claimed that the resulting embeddings can help compress the TCGA dataset because researchers can utilize resulting features intead of original WSIs in various downstream tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
$Strengths$:

1. This paper focuses on applying contrastive learning to two aggregated views of WSI in order to learn slide-level representations. This idea sounds interesting and is easy to implement in practice. 

2. The introduced Giga-SSL achieves consistent performance improvements on six WSI datasets, especially when the data budgets are extremely low.

$Weaknesses$:

1. A lack of descriptions for the proposed "aggregation model". Since this is the main focus of this paper, it should be described in more details. However, the methodology section (sec. 3 Methods) fails to clarify how to build the aggregation model. The authors only claimed that they applied a pooling operator $p_{\theta_2}(\cdot)$ to the resulting embeddings of two views (i.e., $X_1$ and $X_2$). Fig. 1 includes a "sparse ResNet18" that never appears in the main text. Based on the related work, is SparseConvMIL (Lerousseau et al.) used as the sparse cnn? If so, the authors should clarify the differences between their implementation and SparseConvMIL.

2. The submission is hard to read. Lots of statements in the submission are unclear, unsupported, and some of them are incorrect. Here are some examples from the manuscript.

(i) "Whole Slide Images (WSI) are microscopy images of diseased tissue", the first sentence in sec. Introduction, is obviously incorrect because many WSI contain healthy tissue.

(ii)  "The large amount of noise thus often leads to overfitting and poor performance." What kind of noise do you refer to? Label noise or imaging noise? The authors should clarify this statement.

(iii) "Indeed, MIL performance reaches saturation when using thousands of slides with associated ground truth for training." I recommend adding references here because the comment of "performance saturation" should be built upon evidence.

(iv) "While traditional MIL assumes independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) instances within each bag." Again, citation is needed.

(v) "the pretext task seems to be too easy to lead to powerful representations." This is a sentence quoted from sec. 2.3. I'm not clear about the definition of the difficulty of pretext tasks and why an "easy" pretext task fails to provide powerful representations. Also, the phrase "powerful" is not appropriate.

3. Important implementation details are missing. 

(i) Is the pre-trained model fixed or trainable during the pre-training stage?

(ii) What is the number of Tiles ($T$) adopted in each batch? 

(iii) Are sampled tiles overlapped or not? 

(iv) What is the exact batch size in pre-training? How to determine this number as it affects a lot in SimCLR (the contrastive loss that the authors adopted)?

(v) In sec. 3.1, the authors claimed that 50 augmentations are used. What do these augmentations include?

4. The writing is pool, and some typos exist. 

(i) The 4th sentence in sec. 2.1. The first character of "this assumption" should be capitalized.

(ii) In the last sentence of sec. 2.1, it should be $c_{\theta_3}(\cdot)$.

(iii) In sec. 2.3, "Dino" should be DINO.

(iv) "If the tile-level augmentations are shared among the same view." What does "among the same view" mean?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
$Clarity\ and\ Quality$:

As aforementioned, how to aggregate two views of the same WSI is missing. Many statements in the submission lack evidence and literature supports. Besides, implementation details are not sufficient. All these points make the manuscript hard to read, reducing the appeal to interested readers. Thus, I strongly recommend the authors to take some time to carefully polish the draft, which would be helpful to increase the impact of this paper.

$Novelty$:

Personally, I like simple and effective solutions. This is reason why I think the novelty of the proposed Giga-SSL is acceptable, although it seems that Giga-SSL incorporates the ideas of multi-crop (besides, the authors should cite the paper that proposed multi-crop), SimCLR, and SparseConvMIL.

$Reproducibility$:

Based on provided implementation details, it is quite difficult to reproduce Giga-SSL.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the technical novelty is acceptable, I think the current form of the draft is not suitable for publish because of the unsupported statements, missing methodology descriptions, insufficient implementation details, as mentioned above.

content.title: Self-Supervised Extreme Compression of Gigapixel Images
content.TL;DR: We adapted the self-supervised learning framework to learn gigapixels images embeddings and show their linear superiority on several downstream classification tasks.
content.abstract: Whole slide images (WSI) are microscopy images of stained tissue slides routinely prepared for diagnosis and treatment selection in clinical practice. WSI are very large (gigapixel size) and complex (made of up to millions of cells). The current state-of-the-art (SoTA) approach to classify WSI subdivides them into tiles, encodes them by pre-trained networks, and applies Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) to train for specific downstream tasks. However, annotated datasets are often small, typically a few hundred to a few thousand WSI, which may cause overfitting and underperforming models. On the other hand, the number of unannotated WSI is ever increasing, with datasets of tens of thousands (soon to be millions) of images available. Nevertheless, using unannotated WSI is limited due to the challenges of extending self-supervised learning from natural images to WSI. We propose a strategy of slide-level self-supervised learning (SSL) to leverage the large number of images without annotations to infer powerful slide representations. The resulting embeddings allow compression of the whole public WSI dataset available at the Cancer-Genome Atlas (TCGA), one of the most widely used data resources in cancer research, from 16 TB to 23 MB, thus dramatically simplifying future studies in the field of computational pathology in terms of data storage and processing. We show that a linear classifier trained on top of these embeddings maintains or improves previous SoTA performances on various benchmark WSI classification tasks. Finally, we observe that training a classifier on these representations with tiny datasets (e.g. 50 slides) improved performances over SoTA by an average of +6.3 AUC points over all downstream tasks. We further analyze the conditions necessary for such a training framework to succeed, bringing insights into WSI processing.
